name: Digital Signals of Mental Health
title: Digital Signals of Mental Health
answer: Digital signals of mental health cover the passive and active data that phones, wearables and keyboards produce which may relate to mood, sleep, activity and social contact. The field sits inside telemedicine and triage, where such signals are used to flag changes between appointments or to prioritise who is seen first. It overlaps with psychiatry, clinical psychology, sleep medicine and human computer interaction. The signals themselves are not diagnoses, they are measurements that a clinician may weigh alongside a conversation and a history.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Digital signals of mental health cover the passive and active data that phones, wearables and keyboards produce which may relate to mood, sleep, activity and social contact. The field sits inside telemedicine and triage, where such signals are used to flag changes between appointments or to prioritise who is seen first. It overlaps with psychiatry, clinical psychology, sleep medicine and human computer interaction. The signals themselves are not diagnoses, they are measurements that a clinician may weigh alongside a conversation and a history.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The stack is usually a consumer device, a phone or a wrist worn sensor, an app or software development kit that collects the data, and a backend that stores and processes it. Sleep duration, step counts, heart rate variability, typing speed, screen time and voice samples are common inputs. Some systems run inference on the device, others send data to a cloud service.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work typically starts with a labelled dataset linking sensor traces to clinical scores such as the PHQ-9 or GAD-7, gathered in a research or pilot setting. Models are then trained to predict a score or a change in state, and performance is reported against a held out group. In practice the output is a trend or an alert rather than a diagnosis, and a clinician decides what it means. Validation is hard because mood labels are noisy, devices change, and a model tuned on one population often travels poorly to another.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: These tools touch sensitive health data, so consent, data minimisation and clear limits on secondary use are central. In the United States, software that makes a clinical claim can fall under FDA device rules, while general wellness products sit outside them, and state privacy laws add further duties.Provenance matters too, since a signal is only as trustworthy as the device, the sampling rate and the version of the model that produced it.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The near term direction is toward passive monitoring that runs quietly in the background and surfaces only when something changes, with triage tools that help a clinic decide who needs contact first. Better calibration across devices and populations, and clearer rules on what counts as a clinical claim, will shape which products reach patients. Voice and speech markers are an active research area, and so is the question of how to keep a person informed about what their own data suggests. The open problem is not detection alone but what a service does after a signal appears.
